stories.headline: CHIP RALLY LIFTS S&P 500, NASDAQ AHEAD OF NVIDIA'S REPORT WEDNESDAY
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.32% to 7,677 and the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.64% to 29,209 as semiconductor names rallied into Nvidia's after-the-bell earnings Wednesday: AMD +4.3%, Intel +3.2%, Marvell +7.0%, and Nvidia itself snapped a seven-session losing streak with a 2.5% gain. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 7 bps to 4.64%, its second straight daily decline.
stories.explain: Nvidia's results function as a read-through for the entire AI capex cycle, so positioning ahead of the print tends to move the whole semiconductor complex in sympathy rather than just the one stock. The simultaneous yield decline reflects investors rotating into duration ahead of Wednesday's GDP revision and PCE inflation data, both of which will shape how much room the Fed has to cut before its September meeting.

stories.headline: OIL SINKS 5% ON SIGNS OF A STRAIT OF HORMUZ DEAL; GOLD PUSHES TOWARD $4,725
stories.body: WTI crude fell 5.08% to $81 a barrel after reports that Iran and Oman are nearing an agreement to normalize shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, unwinding a geopolitical risk premium built up over five months of periodic attacks and U.S. retaliatory strikes. Gold rose 0.75% to $4,724 an ounce, extending its August rally on persistent U.S. debt-load and dollar-softness concerns.
stories.explain: Oil's move is a repricing of tail risk: traders had built a premium into the barrel for the probability of a chokepoint closure that carries roughly a fifth of global seaborne crude, and that premium can unwind in a single session once the probability resets lower, unlike a gradual supply-demand shift. Gold's steadier climb reflects a separate, slower-moving trade tied to debt and currency debasement rather than today's specific headline, which is why the two safe-haven-adjacent assets are diverging.

stories.headline: TRUMP DOUBLES DOWN, SETS 50% TARIFFS ON CANADIAN AUTOS AND STEEL FOR 2027
stories.body: President Trump announced the U.S. will raise tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel to 50% effective Jan. 1, 2027, doubling the current 25% duty on Canadian auto imports, after trade talks between the two countries collapsed. Canadian steel already faces a 50% levy; the White House says U.S.-built vehicles are exempt.
stories.explain: Tariffs are collected from the U.S. importer of record, so the immediate mechanism is higher input costs passed through to American buyers and automakers unless Canadian exporters cut prices to absorb the hit, which thin-margin sectors like autos and steel have little room to do. Markets are treating the January effective date as a negotiating window rather than a certainty, which is part of why the tariff news moved currency and industrial names more than broad equity indexes today.

stories.headline: FED HOLDS AT 3.5%-3.75%; MARKETS AWAIT WARSH'S FIRST JACKSON HOLE SPEECH FRIDAY
stories.body: The FOMC voted 9-3 to hold its target range at 3.50%-3.75% at its July 28-29 meeting, with Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan dissenting in favor of a hike. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday, three weeks before the Sept. 16 decision, with GDP's second estimate and the PCE Price Index due Wednesday.
stories.explain: A Jackson Hole speech matters less for what it says about the next meeting than for the reaction function it signals: how the Fed will respond to future data, which is why investors are parsing Warsh's tone on a labor market showing cracks against inflation that hasn't fully cooled. Today's cooler energy prices from oil's slide give the Fed more room on the inflation side of that calculus heading into Wednesday's PCE print, which is the last major data point before Warsh speaks.

stories.headline: DICK'S SPORTING GOODS CRATERS 27% AS FOOT LOCKER INTEGRATION DRAGS ON RESULTS
stories.body: Dick's Sporting Goods fell 27% after posting Q2 revenue of $5.59 billion and adjusted EPS of $3.53, both missing Wall Street's roughly $5.64 billion and $3.77 estimates, and cutting full-year guidance to $21.9-$22.2 billion in revenue and about $11.50 in adjusted EPS. Foot Locker, acquired earlier this year, posted a 3.6% comparable-sales decline on heavy discounting even as Dick's namesake stores grew comps 4.9%.
stories.explain: The stock's move is disproportionate to the revenue miss because guidance cuts reprice the entire forward earnings stream, not just one quarter, and the market is now questioning whether the Foot Locker acquisition's integration costs and inventory glut are a one-off or a structural drag. It's a useful read-through for consumer discretionary broadly heading into the holiday season, since heavy discounting to clear athletic inventory signals softer demand than the headline retail sales data has shown.

stories.headline: LOUISIANA JUDGE RULES RJ LUIS ELIGIBLE FOR LSU AS TRANSFER-ELIGIBILITY CHAOS CONTINUES
stories.body: A Louisiana judge ruled that former G-Leaguer RJ Luis is eligible to play this season at LSU under Will Wade, the latest in a wave of state-court rulings granting eligibility outside the NCAA's own process. Elsewhere, Utah's Noam Yaacov was ruled ineligible and will instead pursue a professional career overseas, while Clemson's Dillon Hunter is returning for a fifth season of eligibility.

stories.headline: CLIPPERS, RAPTORS IN TRADE TALKS FOR KAWHI LEONARD AS OFFSEASON SHAKEUP CONTINUES
stories.body: The Clippers and Raptors have been in trade discussions for All-NBA forward Kawhi Leonard for several weeks, per league sources. Elsewhere, the Kings are waiving six-time All-Star DeMar DeRozan after exploring trade routes, instantly making him one of the top remaining names on the 2026 free-agent market, and Rockets guard Fred VanVleet is opting into his $25 million player option for 2026-27.

stories.headline: BROWNS NAME DESHAUN WATSON WEEK 1 STARTER OVER SHEDEUR SANDERS
stories.body: Cleveland named Deshaun Watson its Week 1 starting quarterback over rookie Shedeur Sanders, setting up his first regular-season start since tearing his Achilles in 2024, an injury he later re-tore. Elsewhere, Bengals WR Ja'Marr Chase left Tuesday's practice with what the team called a minor hyperextension of his knee, and the Texans traded for receiver Kayshon Boutte from New England.

stories.headline: COLLEGE FOOTBALL OPENS SATURDAY: KIFFIN'S LSU DEBUT AND PENN STATE'S RESET HEADLINE WEEK 1
stories.body: The 2026 season kicks off this Saturday, the third year of the 12-team College Football Playoff, with Lane Kiffin's move from Ole Miss to LSU and Penn State's rebuild among the top storylines after preseason bowl projections were released Tuesday. Indiana's Curt Cignetti, coming off a perfect 16-0 season, headlines the group of coaches trying to prove last year wasn't a fluke.

sports.detail: Season opens Sept. 6 vs. Washington State, 4 p.m. ET on NBC at Husky Stadium. Head coach Jedd Fisch takes over as offensive play-caller after OC Jimmie Dougherty's February departure; four Huskies landed on major award watch lists this week, including Manu (Polynesian POY) and Williams Jr. (Davey O'Brien).

Finished 16-17 (7-13 Big Ten) last season, missing the NCAA Tournament. Lost top scorer Hannes Steinbach (drafted 14th overall by Charlotte) and No. 2 scorer Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky); Wesley Yates III (13 ppg) returns as the leader of a retooled roster.

Fell to the Titans in Nashville Sunday to go 0-2 in the preseason; face the Chiefs in the preseason finale Friday, Aug. 28 at 8 p.m. ET. Trevon Diggs has joined the roster late in camp, and the NFL's finance and ownership committees have recommended approval of the franchise sale to a group led by Neeru and Vinod Khosla.

The 2026-27 schedule was released this month: Detroit opens at home against the Celtics before a three-game road trip to Miami, Philadelphia, and New York. The offseason focus has been adding ball-handling and 3-point shooting as the Pistons look to defend their Central Division title.

Beat the Phillies 9-2 Monday behind three Cal Raleigh home runs and a three-run shot from Julio Rodriguez, snapping Philadelphia's nine-game winning streak. Seattle is 63-69 on the season; the two teams play again tonight at T-Mobile Park.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote — Friday

deepDive.title: How a Geopolitical Risk Premium Unwinds: Today's Oil Plunge, Explained
content: WTI crude dropped 5% today, the sharpest single-session move in the brief's market strip, on nothing more than reports that Iran and Oman are nearing a deal to normalize shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. No barrel of actual supply changed hands differently than yesterday. What moved was the market's estimate of the probability that a chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of global seaborne crude gets disrupted again, after five months of periodic attacks and U.S. retaliatory strikes had kept that probability elevated. Understanding how that number gets priced in, and how fast it can come back out, is the key to reading today's tape.

Traders don't price oil off current supply and demand alone; they price the futures curve, and a chokepoint risk gets embedded as a premium layered on top of the fundamental price, visible as a wedge between spot and forward-month contracts and in elevated war-risk insurance rates on tankers transiting the strait. That premium is a probability-weighted cost: if there's a 10% chance per month of a disruption that would spike prices $20-$30 a barrel, roughly $2-$3 gets added to today's price to compensate holders for that tail risk. It's a discrete, binary-outcome premium, not a continuous supply-demand adjustment, which is exactly why it can unwind in one session once the market revises the probability down.

This isn't a new pattern. Brent spiked over 10% in hours after the 2019 Abqaiq drone strikes on Saudi processing facilities, and gave most of it back within two weeks once spare capacity proved sufficient. The run-up to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine embedded a similar premium that partially reversed as soon as it became clear Russian barrels would keep flowing through gray-market channels. The tell in each case is the same: a premium built on the fear of a disruption evaporates faster than one built on an actual, realized supply cut, because there's no physical barrel to replace, only a fear to revise.

The mechanism matters beyond energy traders because oil feeds directly into headline PCE and CPI through gasoline and freight costs, and Wednesday's PCE print is the last major data point before Fed Chair Warsh's Friday Jackson Hole speech. A falling energy input gives the Fed more room to describe inflation as well-contained, which is part of why the 10-year yield fell in sympathy with oil today rather than moving independently. The flip side is the same mechanism in reverse: if Strait of Hormuz talks break down before Friday, the premium can reprice into the barrel just as quickly as it left, and with it, some of today's rate-cut optimism.
